37.0.0.en: After Josiah died, killed in the battle of Megiddo, his son “Jehoahaz” reigned for three months, and then the king of Egypt took him captive, and his brother “Jehoiakim” reigned in his place. After “Jehoiakim” the son of Josiah was killed by the king of Babylon, his son “Jehoiachin,” who is also called “Jeconiah” or “Coniah,” reigned for a short time, three months, and then “Nebuchadnezzar” took him captive to Babylon, and his uncle “Zedekiah,” the brother of “Jehoiakim” and the son of “Josiah” the righteous king, reigned in his place. In the reign of “Zedekiah” Jerusalem was destroyed, the temple burned, and the Babylonian captivity began, for Zedekiah was the last king of the kingdom of Judah.

37.0.1.en: It is noticeable that from (chs. 37-44) Jeremiah relates to us many events of his history.

37.1.0.en: It is made clear here that Zedekiah, like his brother Jehoiakim, turned away from the way of God and that both refused to obey Jeremiah, the prophet of God. Although Zedekiah sometimes asked about the word of God, he did not obey it, for his personality was weaker than that of his brother Jehoiakim. Yet both were far from God, and no righteous king arose over the kingdom of Judah after Josiah.

37.2.0.en: Zedekiah was in perplexity whether to ally himself with the king of Egypt or submit to the king of Babylon, so he sent two of his aides to Jeremiah to pray for him and guide him.

37.3.0.en: At this time Jeremiah enjoyed freedom of movement among the people and spoke to them the word of God, that is, he had not yet been cast into prison.

37.3.1.en: If you have a position or leadership or authority, do not forget that it is God who gave you all this. So seek Him and obey His commandments, and you will live in reassurance and lead those with you in the straight way.

37.3.3.en: 5- Then Pharaoh's army was come forth out of Egypt: and when the Chaldeans that besieged Jerusalem heard tidings of them, they departed from Jerusalem. 6- Then came the word of the LORD unto the prophet Jeremiah, saying, 7- Thus saith the LORD, the God of Israel; Thus shall ye say to the king of Judah, that sent you unto me to enquire of me; Behold, Pharaoh's army, which is come forth to help you, shall return to Egypt into their own land. 8- And the Chaldeans shall come again, and fight against this city, and take it, and burn it with fire.

37.3.4.en: 9- Thus saith the LORD; Deceive not yourselves, saying, The Chaldeans shall surely depart from us: for they shall not depart.

37.3.5.en: 10- For though ye had smitten the whole army of the Chaldeans that fight against you, and there remained but wounded men among them, yet should they rise up every man in his tent, and burn this city with fire.

37.4.0.en: The army of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem in the year 588 BC, and “Hophra” king of Egypt, the son of Necho, was afraid of Babylon's attacking Egypt. So he moved with his armies, not out of love for the Jews but in defense of his own country, and came out to attack the army of Babylon besieging Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar feared fighting two armies, the army of Egypt and the army of Jerusalem, and preferred to fight each of them separately so that victory over it would be easy for him, and for this reason he withdrew at that time from fighting Jerusalem. This left King Zedekiah in perplexity as to which was stronger, so as to ally himself with it and submit to it: the king of Egypt or the king of Babylon?

37.5.0.en: God sent Jeremiah a prophecy answering the question of King Zedekiah, and he told his envoys that the army of Egypt would withdraw and move away from Jerusalem and return to Egypt.

37.6.0.en: Then Jeremiah added in his prophecy that the army of Babylon had left Jerusalem temporarily and would return to besiege it, take it, destroy it and burn it with fire.

37.7.0.en: Jeremiah warned Zedekiah and those with him not to deceive themselves and think that Babylon would not return, since Zedekiah wished for this and wanted an alliance with Egypt. But Jeremiah assured them that Nebuchadnezzar would return and take the city.

37.7.1.en: No one can deceive you unless you deceive yourself and accept the evil thoughts of the devil. So submit to God's commandments and repent of your sins, and the Holy Spirit will give you discernment and guidance.

37.8.0.en: Jeremiah also added that if they overcame Babylon and nothing remained of its army except a small number of wounded men, pierced with spears and struck by arrows, even so they would rise up and be able to take Jerusalem and destroy it; that is, the Chaldeans, or the Babylonians, will certainly destroy Jerusalem.

37.8.2.en: 11- And it came to pass, that when the army of the Chaldeans was broken up from Jerusalem for fear of Pharaoh's army, 12- Then Jeremiah went forth out of Jerusalem to go into the land of Benjamin, to separate himself thence in the midst of the people. 13- And when he was in the gate of Benjamin, a captain of the ward was there, whose name was Irijah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Hananiah; and he took Jeremiah the prophet, saying, Thou fallest away to the Chaldeans. 14- Then said Jeremiah, It is false; I fall not away to the Chaldeans. But he hearkened not to him: so Irijah took Jeremiah, and brought him to the princes. 15- Wherefore the princes were wroth with Jeremiah, and smote him, and put him in prison in the house of Jonathan the scribe: for they had made that the prison. 16- When Jeremiah was entered into the dungeon, and into the cabins, and Jeremiah had remained there many days;

37.9.0.en: After the armies of Babylon feared the army of Egypt and lifted the siege from Jerusalem and returned to Babylon, the Jews of Jerusalem felt relief and went out to look at their fields around Jerusalem and attend to their trade and affairs. The prophet Jeremiah went out with them to look at his field that he had bought in Anathoth, which lies north of Jerusalem and is his town where he was born. He had bought this field when he was imprisoned and had not seen it. He went out amid the crowd, thinking that no one would pay attention to him among the many going out of Jerusalem.

37.10.0.en: The gate of Benjamin: one of the gates of Jerusalem, lying on its north side and leading to the land where the tribe of Benjamin lived.

37.10.1.en: The captain of the ward: the chief of the guards who guard the city of Jerusalem.

37.10.2.en: You fall away to the Chaldeans: you go out to meet the Chaldeans with whom you are allied.

37.10.3.en: As Jeremiah was going out of Jerusalem, Irijah the captain of the ward saw him and seized him, accusing him of betraying his country and going out to meet the Babylonian enemies. Irijah thought this because Jeremiah's prophecies called for submission to Babylon.

37.11.0.en: Jeremiah tried to defend himself and deny the accusation directed at him, but Irijah did not accept his defense and seized him and brought him to the leaders of the people.

37.12.0.en: It appears here that the princes in the days of King Zedekiah were wicked, rejecting the word of God, and differed from the pious princes who were in the days of Jehoiakim, mentioned in the previous chapter. The princes ordered Jeremiah to be cast into the prison that was in the house of the king's official scribe, who was called Jonathan, and this was after they had beaten Jeremiah.

37.13.0.en: The cistern: a pit or a lower chamber in the depth of the earth.

37.13.1.en: The vaults: the cistern had vaults above the ground.

37.13.2.en: They put Jeremiah in and left him a long time in the prison of the house of Jonathan, which is the vaulted cistern.

37.13.3.en: Do not be disturbed by the false accusations that the world directs at you, nor by its wrongs, however severe, because God is with you. Even if you are alone, God supports you and shows your right in the end and rewards you for all your labors.

37.13.4.en: [4] The release of Jeremiah and his plea for mercy (vv. 17-21)

37.13.5.en: 17- Then Zedekiah the king sent, and took him out: and the king asked him secretly in his house, and said, Is there any word from the LORD? And Jeremiah said, There is: for, said he, thou shalt be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon. 18- Moreover Jeremiah said unto king Zedekiah, What have I offended against thee, or against thy servants, or against this people, that ye have put me in prison? 19- Where are now your prophets which prophesied unto you, saying, The king of Babylon shall not come against you, nor against this land? 20- Therefore hear now, I pray thee, O my lord the king: let my supplication, I pray thee, be accepted before thee; that thou cause me not to return to the house of Jonathan the scribe, lest I die there. 21- Then Zedekiah the king commanded that they should commit Jeremiah into the court of the prison, and that they should give him daily a piece of bread out of the bakers' street, until all the bread in the city were spent. Thus Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison.

37.14.0.en: King Zedekiah thought that prison might affect Jeremiah and change his opinion, forgetting that it was God who was speaking and not Jeremiah. And because Zedekiah's desire, his wish that the Chaldeans would not return, controlled his heart, he sent secretly and brought Jeremiah to his palace and asked to hear the word of God. Jeremiah did not fear the king's violence and made light of the sufferings, and proclaimed the voice of God strongly and clearly, namely that the Chaldeans would take Jerusalem and destroy it.

37.14.1.en: Do not be afraid to proclaim the truth, however difficult your circumstances or evident your weakness, because God is with you, upholding you and protecting you. Give Him the opportunity to speak through your mouth; seek Him, and He will guide you and strengthen you.

37.15.0.en: Jeremiah rebuked King Zedekiah because they had cast him into the hard prison, which is the cistern, and asked the king what sin he had committed that he was cast into the cistern, because he had not been tried before being cast into the cistern.

37.16.0.en: He also rebuked the king, showing the falsehood of the false prophets around the king who said that the king of Babylon would not attack Jerusalem, whereas the opposite happened, for Jerusalem had been besieged and would be besieged again and they would take it. This siege proves the truthfulness of Jeremiah's prophecies.

37.17.0.en: It appears that the prison of Jonathan, that is, the cistern, was very harsh, so that it could not be endured for long. It was probably very damp and dark. So Jeremiah asked King Zedekiah and begged him not to return him to this prison, especially as he was innocent.

37.18.0.en: Until all the bread in the city were spent: however severe the famine in Jerusalem became. The bakers' street: an area or street in which ovens and bakers were gathered in the city of Jerusalem, as is the case in many cities of the world where there are streets and markets for certain crafts and products. King Zedekiah was affected by Jeremiah's words and felt his innocence and sympathized with him, but he was weak in personality, so he could not order his release lest the leaders of the people who opposed Jeremiah rise up against him. He contented himself with moving him to a better prison, the one in the king's palace, and ordered that he be given food every day however much hunger prevailed in Jerusalem, because it was expected because of the Babylonian siege that was coming upon them. The mire in the cistern

38.0.0.en: Here are mentioned the names of four of the king's princes, two of whom were mentioned before, one in (ch. 37:3) and the other in (ch. 21:1). We notice a great similarity between the events of chapters 37 and 38, which declares that the two chapters concern the same events, but each chapter mentions details that clarify what happened with Jeremiah. The devoting of two chapters to the same event shows its importance, for it shows the following:

38.0.1.en: 1- The ingratitude of the princes and the people and their resistance to God, represented in Jeremiah.

38.0.2.en: 2- Jeremiah, the servant of God, endured many labors for the sake of his ministry.

38.0.3.en: 3- The steadfastness of Jeremiah's faith unto death.

38.0.4.en: 4- The cruelty of the princes, which reached the point of trying to kill Jeremiah.

38.0.5.en: 5- The weakness of King Zedekiah's personality before the princes.

38.0.6.en: 6- The evil of Zedekiah and his inclination to be rid of Jeremiah, but at the hand of others.

38.1.0.en: He that goeth forth to the Chaldeans: he surrenders himself to the Chaldeans. Jeremiah called them to surrender themselves to the Chaldeans, but if they remained in Jerusalem they would die by one of these means:

38.1.1.en: 1- Being killed by the sword at the hand of the Chaldeans.

38.1.2.en: 2- Dying of hunger because the food ran out.

38.1.3.en: 3- Dying of disease because epidemics had spread among the people, helped by the corpses thrown in the streets.

38.2.0.en: Jeremiah declared that Jerusalem would fall into the hand of the Chaldeans and they would take it.

38.3.0.en: When the king's princes learned of Jeremiah's prophecy, they decided that he was a traitor and an agent of the Chaldeans and that these words of his made the Jewish fighters doubt victory over the Chaldeans, so that they would weaken before them, and thus Jerusalem would fall into the hand of the Chaldeans. And because he was against the Jews, they decided to kill him.

38.4.0.en: The weakness of Zedekiah appears here in his yielding to the decision of the princes and leaving Jeremiah in their hand to do with him what they wished. This shows two things:

38.4.2.en: 2- His heart may have been evil and wanted to be rid of Jeremiah and his prophecies, but at the hand of others, the princes.

38.5.0.en: The princes carried out the sentence of death on Jeremiah by casting him into the cistern of Malchiah the king's son, which is probably the one mentioned in chapter 37 as being in the house of Jonathan, that is, beside it. This cistern had no water but mire to a great depth, the amount of which is not mentioned, and life in this cistern was impossible, because if he slept he would be suffocated by the mire and die.

38.5.1.en: Be strong and proclaim the voice of God however much people threaten you, and trust that He protects you even if you draw near to death. Indeed, He frightens your enemies, glorifies you and rewards you for your steadfastness.

38.5.2.en: [2] The rescue of Jeremiah from the cistern (vv. 7-13)

38.5.3.en: 7- Now when Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, one of the eunuchs which was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the dungeon; the king then sitting in the gate of Benjamin; 8- Ebedmelech went forth out of the king's house, and spake to the king, saying, 9- My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet, whom they have cast into the dungeon; and he is like to die for hunger in the place where he is: for there is no more bread in the city. 10- Then the king commanded Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, saying, Take from hence thirty men with thee, and take up Jeremiah the prophet out of the dungeon, before he die. 11- So Ebedmelech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took thence old cast clouts and old rotten rags, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah.

38.5.4.en: 12- And Ebedmelech the Ethiopian said unto Jeremiah, Put now these old cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes under the cords. And Jeremiah did so. 13- So they drew up Jeremiah with cords, and took him up out of the dungeon: and Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison.

38.6.0.en: Ebedmelech the Ethiopian: one of the servants of the king of Judah who were close to him, and his origin was from Cush, that is, Ethiopia.

38.6.1.en: A eunuch, who was in the king's house: he was probably in the house of the women, since eunuchs were employed to serve the king's women.

38.6.2.en: One of the king's servants, called Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, who was probably assigned to serve the house of the king's women, heard that the wicked princes had put Jeremiah in the cistern full of mire, and he took pity on him. Perhaps the king's women told him of this and they too took pity on Jeremiah. So he tried to rescue Jeremiah from dying of hunger in the damp cistern full of mire, and he looked for the king to speak to him and found him sitting near one of the northern gates of Jerusalem, which is called the gate of Benjamin. This shows that the servant of the king had tender feelings and likewise believed the word of God through the mouth of Jeremiah. So he went to the king to speak to him about rescuing Jeremiah.

38.7.0.en: The courage of Ebedmelech also appears here, for he was not afraid of the king's princes who had put Jeremiah in the cistern, and he declared to the king that Jeremiah would certainly die because he had no food, in addition to the hardness of life in the cistern because of the damp and the mire. He added a matter that perhaps troubled the king, which, as the Septuagint translation of this verse makes clear, is that the death of Jeremiah by hunger would bring hunger and evil on all of Jerusalem as well. Perhaps Ebedmelech based this conclusion of his on the fact that wronging a man of God brings the anger of God upon Jerusalem.

38.8.0.en: King Zedekiah was affected by Ebedmelech's words, either out of pity for Jeremiah, but probably out of fear of the evil that would come upon Jerusalem because of Jeremiah's death. So he allowed Ebedmelech to bring Jeremiah out of the cistern, and even commanded him to take thirty men with him to bring Jeremiah up. By this he meant that he should not meet resistance from the wicked princes, that is, that he should have a force with him so that these princes would be afraid.

38.8.1.en: Jeremiah here is a type of Christ, whom the Jews killed. That is, they lowered Jeremiah into the cistern to die, rejecting his teachings, but the Gentiles, whom Ebedmelech the Ethiopian signifies, believed in the Resurrection of Christ, which is signified by the bringing up of Jeremiah from the cistern.

38.9.0.en: The tenderness of Ebedmelech and the delicacy of his feelings appear here. He did not let down ropes to Jeremiah and bring him up with them lest his body be wounded, but took worn-out, that is, old, clothes and let them down to Jeremiah so that he might put them under his armpits and they would protect him from any wounds the ropes might cause. Jeremiah did as Ebedmelech told him, and they brought him up from the cistern and moved him to an ordinary prison above ground in the king's house, and so he saved him from death.

38.9.1.en: May you feel the suffering of those around you and try to help them. Sympathize with them and encourage them and try to connect them to Christ and the Church, and rescue them from their hardships with all your strength, and God will rejoice in your love. [3] Jeremiah's meeting with Zedekiah (vv. 14-23)

38.9.2.en: 14- Then Zedekiah the king sent, and took Jeremiah the prophet unto him into the third entry that is in the house of the LORD: and the king said unto Jeremiah, I will ask thee a thing; hide nothing from me. 15- Then Jeremiah said unto Zedekiah, If I declare it unto thee, wilt thou not surely put me to death? and if I give thee counsel, wilt thou not hearken unto me? 16- So Zedekiah the king sware secretly unto Jeremiah, saying, As the LORD liveth, that made us this soul, I will not put thee to death, neither will I give thee into the hand of these men that seek thy life.

38.9.3.en: 17- Then said Jeremiah unto Zedekiah, Thus saith the LORD, the God of hosts, the God of Israel; If thou wilt assuredly go forth unto the king of Babylon's princes, then thy soul shall live, and this city shall not be burned with fire; and thou shalt live, and thine house: 18- But if thou wilt not go forth to the king of Babylon's princes, then shall this city be given into the hand of the Chaldeans, and they shall burn it with fire, and thou shalt not escape out of their hand.

38.9.4.en: 19- And Zedekiah the king said unto Jeremiah, I am afraid of the Jews that are fallen to the Chaldeans, lest they deliver me into their hand, and they mock me. 20- But Jeremiah said, They shall not deliver thee. Obey, I beseech thee, the voice of the LORD, which I speak unto thee: so it shall be well unto thee, and thy soul shall live. 21- But if thou refuse to go forth, this is the word that the LORD hath shewed me: 22- And, behold, all the women that are left in the king of Judah's house shall be brought forth to the king of Babylon's princes, and those women shall say, Thy friends have set thee on, and have prevailed against thee: thy feet are sunk in the mire, and they are turned away back. 23- So they shall bring out all thy wives and thy children to the Chaldeans: and thou shalt not escape out of their hand, but shalt be taken by the hand of the king of Babylon: and thou shalt cause this city to be burned with fire.

38.10.0.en: The third entry: perhaps an entrance reserved for the king into the house of the Lord.

38.10.1.en: King Zedekiah was afraid and felt the nearness of the end, which he understood from Jeremiah's earlier words, and he was no longer sure of the words of his false prophets. So he sent to summon Jeremiah from the prison to hear the word of God from him.

38.11.0.en: Jeremiah was courageous in telling the king the voice of God, but he rebuked the king before telling him what would happen. He said to him that if he told him the voice of God and it was against him, he might kill him or leave the princes to kill him, because Zedekiah was weak in personality and might make light of God's word and not obey it because of the weakness of his faith.

38.12.0.en: The king promised Jeremiah that he would not leave him in the hand of the princes to kill him; that is, he declared his concern to hear the voice of God and promised to preserve Jeremiah's life.

38.13.0.en: Jeremiah proclaimed the voice of God, whom he described as the LORD of hosts, that is, the strong One, able to do all things, and advised the king to surrender himself to the Chaldeans and live. Here the love of Jeremiah appears for the king who had wronged him, for he seeks his salvation and deliverance from death. But if Zedekiah did not listen to the word of God, a great evil would occur, which he summarizes in five punishments:

38.13.1.en: 1- The taking of Jerusalem by Babylon.

38.14.0.en: He continues the punishments and says:

38.14.1.en: 3- The seizing of Zedekiah by Nebuchadnezzar when he tries to flee.

38.15.0.en: King Zedekiah showed his fear of the Jews allied with Nebuchadnezzar, who had gone out from Jerusalem and gone to Nebuchadnezzar, lest they seize him and hand him over to him.

38.16.0.en: Jeremiah reassured Zedekiah that the Jews who were allies of Nebuchadnezzar would not hand him over to him, but when Zedekiah surrendered himself to Nebuchadnezzar, he would treat him well and not kill him.

38.17.0.en: It is understood from this verse that Jeremiah had seen a vision that made clear to him what would happen at Nebuchadnezzar's attack on Jerusalem. He explained its details in the two following verses.

38.18.0.en: The vision makes clear the remaining punishments that will come upon Zedekiah if he does not obey God, which are:

38.18.1.en: 4- The seizing of all the king's women by the princes of Nebuchadnezzar.

38.18.2.en: 5- The rebuke of Zedekiah by his women because he relied on the false prophets, so these disasters befell him and them, instead of his submitting to God, who spoke through the mouth of Jeremiah.

38.18.3.en: They liken his falling into the hand of the Babylonians to his sinking in the mire from which he cannot get out, that is, the mire of bondage and humiliation. This shows that Jeremiah, because he is a man of God, was rescued from the mire, whereas Zedekiah, because of his not submitting to God, fell into the mire, that is, the bondage of Nebuchadnezzar, and did not come out of it.

38.18.4.en: Do not resist God's commandments, for they are your good and your benefit even if they seem illogical or hard, because they rescue you from destruction and from the hand of Satan.

38.18.6.en: 24- Then said Zedekiah unto Jeremiah, Let no man know of these words, and thou shalt not die. 25- But if the princes hear that I have talked with thee, and they come unto thee, and say unto thee, Declare unto us now what thou hast said unto the king, hide it not from us, and we will not put thee to death; also what the king said unto thee: 26- Then thou shalt say unto them, I presented my supplication before the king, that he would not cause me to return to Jonathan's house, to die there.

38.18.7.en: 27- Then came all the princes unto Jeremiah, and asked him: and he told them according to all these words that the king had commanded. So they left off speaking with him; for the matter was not perceived. 28- So Jeremiah abode in the court of the prison until the day that Jerusalem was taken: and when Jerusalem was taken

38.19.0.en: The king was afraid of his princes, lest they learn of the punishments coming upon Jerusalem and rise up and kill Jeremiah, regarding him as an ally of Babylon and an adversary of his people. This means that Zedekiah had begun to be convinced by Jeremiah's words, but did not have the full faith and the courage to carry them out. He represents the person weak in personality and weak in faith who wavers between life with God and the thoughts of the world.

38.20.0.en: The king told Jeremiah that the princes would certainly hear of your meeting with me. He knew that they had spies among the king's aides and that they would summon Jeremiah and ask him about what took place in the meeting. He guided him to mention a part of what took place in the meeting, namely Jeremiah's request to the king not to return him to the cistern, that is, the prison of Jonathan, so that he would not die. Jeremiah may actually have asked this of the king, or it is understood from what is mentioned in (v. 15), for by the king's killing him he may mean returning him to the cistern if he became angry with him because of his harsh prophecy.

38.21.0.en: The matter was not perceived: Jeremiah's prophecies that he told the king, which include five punishments, were not known to the princes, and therefore they did not become angry with him.

38.21.1.en: The princes indeed went to Jeremiah in the prison and asked him about what took place in the meeting, and he told them as the king had told him, so they left him because they did not know the truth that would anger them.

38.22.0.en: Jeremiah remained in the king's prison until Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem, and this was God's provision for Jeremiah for the following reasons:

38.22.1.en: 1- To rescue Jeremiah from the hand of the princes, who might kill him as their enemy and an ally of Nebuchadnezzar.

38.22.2.en: 2- So that Jeremiah would not see with his own eyes the fall of his beloved city and its destruction.

38.22.3.en: God keeps you and delivers you from many dangers through the afflictions that you pass through, so do not be disturbed by them but accept them, and you will find your salvation.

38.22.4.en: The fall of Jerusalem and its captivity
